Laryngopharyngeal symptoms (LPS) encompass several atypical symptoms that are poorly responsive to PPI, including chronic cough, hoarse voice, throat clearing, sore throat, and excessive phlegm in the throat. 24 , 25 Retrograde movement of gastric contents is rarely demonstrated, making laryngopharyngeal reflux disease infrequent in LPS presentations ( Table 2 ). 26 and alternative mechanisms are more likely. 27 In randomized controlled trials, PPI therapy has shown no significant benefit over placebo in undifferentiated LPS as well as uninvestigated chronic cough, 28 , 29 and abnormal reflux is more likely when typical reflux symptoms coexist with LPS. 30 Both Lyon Consensus 2.0 and the San Diego Consensus for LPS/laryngopharyngeal reflux disease recommend objective upfront esophageal testing prior to anti-reflux therapy for isolated LPS, 5 , 25 which is further supported by cost benefit analysis. 31

In contrast to other LPS, globus is negatively associated with conclusive GERD (OR, 0.5; 95% CI, 0.30-0.86) and has been validated as a negative GERD predictor in a weighted scoring system. 32 Belching may associate with reflux events, but can also be part of behavioral syndromes, making upfront pH-impedance monitoring a useful initial approach ( Table 2 ). 33 Other isolated foregut symptoms such as nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, and dysphagia have very low likelihood of objective GERD, and reflux testing serves primarily to rule out a reflux based mechanism. 5 The more atypical the symptom, the higher the need for documentation of GERD prior to management, as non-GERD etiologies including DGBI and behavioral syndromes are likely to contribute to symptom burden more often than reflux mechanisms.

Therefore, given competing mechanisms and substantial overlap with non-reflux etiologies, troublesome symptoms alone do not define phenotypes with mucosal injury or abnormal acid burden. 34 DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION Diagnostic evaluation becomes necessary in patients with typical symptoms who fail to respond to empiric treatment trials, in patients with LPS or other atypical symptoms, and in the presence of alarm symptoms, where a high-quality upper endoscopy is typically the first test performed ( Table 2 ). 5 , 24 , 35

Although endoscopy is an important tool for the evaluation of esophageal changes from reflux, erosive esophagitis can be identified in only a third of treatment naïve patients with typical reflux symptoms, and the diagnostic yield decreases to < 10% in patients on PPIs despite persistent symptoms. 36 Since erosive esophagitis is expected to heal in > 70% treated with PPIs and > 90% with potassium competitive acid blockers, 37 endoscopic evaluation is recommended off therapy for 2-4 weeks if GERD diagnosis is uncertain. 38,39 Screening for BE is recommended in high-risk populations including patients with chronic GERD symptoms and risk factors including older age, Caucasian race, obesity, family history of esophageal cancer, and tobacco/alcohol use. 40 - 43

Reflux monitoring technology has advanced beyond 24-hour pH measurements alone to include impedance monitoring that can quantify mucosal integrity, and prolonged wireless pH monitoring that records acid burden for up to 96 hours. In patients with unproven GERD and negative endoscopy, ambulatory reflux monitoring off antisecretory therapy differentiates NERD from non-GERD syndromes including RH and FH ( Figure ), using either prolonged wireless pH monitoring or 24-hour catheter based pH/pH-impedance monitoring. 5 The wireless pH probe can be placed during initial diagnostic endoscopy, overcomes day-to-day variability in reflux burden and does not interfere with the patient’s daily activities that might confound 24-hour studies. 44 However, wireless pH monitoring may not be universally available, comes with higher cost, and lacks impedance-based metrics that improve sensitivity and specificity of reflux monitoring. 5 Catheter based pH/pH-impedance monitoring requires high-resolution manometry (HRM) for identification of the proximal margin of the LES for proper placement. This has higher sensitivity in detection of not just acidic but also weakly/non-acidic reflux events, adding to the value of reflux-symptom association. Baseline impedance, a longitudinal marker of esophageal mucosal integrity, can be measured as an adjunctive metric of reflux burden. 5 Further, pH-impedance monitoring on optimized antisecretory therapy can help determine the mechanism of persisting symptoms despite therapy in patients with conclusive GERD. 45

Although insufficient for a conclusive GERD diagnosis by itself, HRM can assess esophageal peristaltic performance, motility patterns associated with reflux and EGJ morphology. 46 , 47 Intact primary esophageal peristalsis helps promptly clear refluxate from the esophagus after reflux events, and brings neutralizing saliva for recovery of mucosal acidification. 16 Hypomotility disorders such as ineffective esophageal motility and absent contractility can prolong contact of the noxious refluxate with esophageal mucosa, potentially causing reflux symptoms and mucosal complications. 48 HRM is an essential component of pre-operative evaluation prior to anti-reflux intervention, 46 when achalasia and obstructive motor disorders mimicking GERD were found in approximately 3% of > 1000 patients being evaluated for anti-reflux surgery. 49

Barium esophagography lacks diagnostic accuracy in identifying conclusive GERD and does not replace ambulatory reflux monitoring in GERD diagnosis. A recent retrospective evaluation of 182 patients who underwent both barium esophagram and ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring found low sensitivity (37.6%) and specificity (71.6%) of barium radiography in diagnosing conclusive GERD according to Lyon Consensus 2.0 criteria. 50 The role of barium esophagography in GERD presentations is primarily in characterizing EGJ morphology, and as an adjunctive study in defining achalasia or other obstructive processes. 46 , 47 MUCOSAL INJURY PHENOTYPES

The Montreal Consensus first outlined syndromes of esophageal injury including reflux esophagitis, peptic stricture, and BE to define end organ complications from GERD ( Figure ). 2 The Lyon Consensus adopted these mucosal injury phenotypes as endoscopic criteria for conclusive GERD ( Table 1 ). 4

Visible erosions in the distal esophageal mucosa remain the most reliable endoscopic findings of acid injury. The Los Angeles (LA) classification assigns higher grades to more profound mucosal injury, which in turn associate with higher acid exposure time (AET) on reflux monitoring, worse symptom severity at baseline, and greater symptom improvement with antisecretory therapy. 51 , 52 While endoscopic healing with antisecretory therapy occurs more often in lower LA grades of esophagitis, 38 , 53 recurrence of esophagitis after withdrawal of therapy is more likely in higher LA grades. 54 The updated Lyon Consensus 2.0 elevated LA grade B esophagitis to conclusive GERD evidence, in light of studies demonstrating similar reflux evidence on pH-impedance testing and response to PPI compared to LA grade C esophagitis, but markedly higher reflux burden than LA grade A esophagitis. 52 , 55 However, interobserver variation in assigning LA grades can confound Lyon Consensus designation of conclusive GERD, 56 , 57 and borderline LA grade B with limited erosions may need to be interpreted similar to LA grade A esophagitis. 58

Peptic esophageal strictures remain an important mucosal injury phenotype, although prevalence has decreased with widespread PPI use. 59 , 60 Peptic strictures are short (< 2 cm), manifest with or without concurrent esophagitis, and typically present with troublesome dysphagia. 61 Biopsies can to rule out alternative mechanisms such as eosinophilic esophagitis or neoplasia. Acid suppression alters the natural history of peptic strictures, and PPIs have been shown to be superior to histamine-2 receptor blockers for resolution of dysphagia, prevention of recurrence, and need for repeated dilation. 62

Salmon colored mucosa in the distal esophagus raises suspicion of BE, and biopsies showing intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells is required to confirm BE in most but not all international guidelines. 41,63 Patients with BE have higher reflux burden compared to healthy volunteers, as well as patients with NERD and erosive esophagitis. 64,65 Long-segment BE (> 3 cm) associates with higher AET, greater number of total reflux episodes, more proximal reflux, and longer acid clearance time. 64 , 66 , 67 Professional societies vary on inclusion of ultrashort segment (< 1 cm) BE and irregular Z line in the BE diagnostic pool, since large retrospective studies show negligible risk of progression to high grade dysplasia or esophageal adenocarcinoma. 68 , 69 However, a recent retrospective study of 167 US veterans with ultrashort segment BE on index endoscopy found persistence of BE in over half of patients, and definitive dysplasia in 8.4% on follow up 70 ; thus exclusion from diagnostic criteria is controversial. 71 Given these discrepancies, the Lyon Consensus 2.0 requires biopsy proven BE for conclusive GERD diagnosis, but makes no specifications regarding BE length, and leaves this designation to the treating physician or surgeon. 5

ABNORMAL REFLUX BURDEN PHENOTYPES When endoscopic evidence of mucosal injury is not evident, further investigation using ambulatory reflux monitoring can segregate NERD from non-GERD phenotypes ( Table 1 ). 6 Meta-analysis of patients with heartburn treated with PPI found similar rates of complete symptom response between erosive esophagitis (72.0%) and NERD with abnormal reflux burden (73.5%), while negative endoscopy without further evaluation had a lower heartburn response (50.5%). 70

Rome V criteria and Lyon Consensus 2.0 both require abnormal AET on either wireless or catheter-based pH/pH impedance monitoring to define NERD. 5 , 9 Cohort studies have consistently demonstrated total AET as the most reproducible metric from ambulatory reflux monitoring, with high sensitivity (77-100%) and specificity (85-100%) for differentiation of patients with esophagitis from healthy controls. 72 - 75 and for predicting symptom improvement after medical or surgical management. 76 The 95th percentile AET threshold lies between 5.3% and 6.3% in healthy controls. 77 - 79 Based on these and other studies comparing acid burden across the GERD spectrum to healthy controls, the AET threshold for pathologic GERD was set at 6% for Western populations, while AET < 4% is considered physiologic, and values 4-6% are inconclusive and require additional supportive data. 4 , 72 In Asian countries, a lower AET threshold of 4% is used to define conclusive GERD. 80

The Lyon Consensus 2.0 suggests prolonged wireless pH testing as the preferred ambulatory modality for evaluation of typical symptoms and negative endoscopy, especially perceptive symptoms (heartburn, esophageal chest pain) ( Table 2 ). In a retrospective study of PPI refractory patients, 85% of patients with discordant results on days 1 and 2 had a predominant physiologic, pathologic or borderline pattern evident with additional days of analysis. 81 Utilizing an AET threshold of < 4% on all days of a 96-hour wireless study, a negative predictive value of 99% was demonstrated in discriminating healthy controls from patients with erosive esophagitis. 52 Additionally, the cumulative number of days with total AET < 4% has added prognostic value in predicting PPI discontinuation. 82

In patients with borderline total AET (4-6%), presence of adjunctive criteria can increase confidence in the likelihood of GERD ( Table 1 ). While various reflux episode thresholds have been reported, 83 ≥ 80 total reflux episodes off acid suppression on pH-impedance monitoring provides the strongest evidence for escalating reflux management. 84 High numbers of total reflux episodes can differentiate PPI dependent GERD patients from healthy controls and a reduction of reflux episodes to below physiologic thresholds post intervention is associated with satisfaction with therapy. 84 , 85 Post hoc analysis of 123 patients randomized to twice daily PPI versus magnetic sphincter augmentation in patients with troublesome regurgitation found that > 80 total reflux episodes predicted satisfaction (≥ 50% reduction of symptoms) with intervention in 31 PPI non-responders who crossed over to magnetic sphincter augmentation. 84

Baseline impedance on pH impedance monitoring is an indicator of esophageal mucosal integrity that can segregate GERD from healthy controls and provide discriminative value in patients with borderline AET. 86 - 88 Mean nocturnal baseline impedance (MNBI) is the average at the 3 cm or 5 cm impedance channel over three 10-minute overnight intervals (1 AM, 2 AM, and 3 AM). Low MNBI (< 1500 Ω) is found in many patients with pathologic or borderline AET but is rare in healthy controls. 81 In a retrospective study of 371 patients who underwent pH impedance monitoring off therapy, symptomatic improvement was similar between patients with pathologic AET and those with borderline AET with low MNBI (73% vs 76%) but similar to physiologic AET when MNBI was normal (33.3% vs 38.6%). 89

Reflux symptom association (RSA) using symptom association probability ( > 95%) and symptom index ( > 50%) assesses temporal relationships between reported symptoms and reflux events. 76 Rome V utilizes RSA in the diagnosis of RH irrespective of response to anti-secretory therapy ( Table 1 ). RSA may provide insights into response to anti-reflux therapy, 90 however, interpretation requires caution and should be used in conjunction with other supporting evidence prior to escalation of anti-reflux therapy. 91 , 92

Mucosal biopsies have a limited role in the diagnosis of GERD. Small studies have shown that microscopic esophagitis is less common in healthy controls and patients with FH (13% and 15% respectively) compared to patients with erosive esophagitis, NERD, and esophageal hypersensitivity (95%, 77%, and 65%, respectively). 93 Dilated intracellular spaces on electron microscopy are more frequent in patients with increased reflux burden (60%) compared to patients with FH (9%), and correlate negatively with MNBI (r = -0.230), however, this technology is not readily available in most clinical settings. 94 Overall, diagnostic performance of histopathology to differentiate conclusive GERD from non-GERD phenotypes is suboptimal and not recommended. 95

NORMAL REFLUX BURDEN PHENOTYPES Rome Diagnoses When AET is physiologic (< 4%) in symptomatic patients, E-DGBI, particularly functional chest pain, FH and RH, are diagnosed using ROME criteria ( Figure ). 9 Patients with heartburn or esophageal chest pain for at least 6 months, without a structural, mucosal or motor disorder on esophageal testing and physiologic acid exposure with no RSA fulfil criteria for FH and functional chest pain. If RSA is present, RH is diagnosed.

Diagnosis of E-DGBI could be confounded by day-to-day variation in reflux burden if reflux monitoring is performed using 24-hour pH-impedance, and with lack of impedance-based markers if wireless pH monitoring is utilized. Some patients with physiologic AET could have adjunctive pH-impedance based metrics that are not within physiologic range. For instance, very low MNBI and/or high reflux episode counts in the context of physiologic AET could raise suspicion of GERD, and indeed, patients fulfilling these criteria demonstrate PPI response. 96 In contrast, patients with AET < 4% and no adjunctive GERD feature (normal baseline impedance, normal reflux episode counts) have psychological profiles and PPI response similar to true functional disorders, which are treated with neuromodulators and adjunctive measures.

Behavioral Phenotypes Patients with regurgitation and belching should be carefully evaluated to discriminate between reflux-related mechanisms, behavioral phenotypes, and overlap between the 2 mechanisms.

Distinction between supragastric belching (SGB), gastric belching, and aerophagia can be made with a combination of HRM with impedance and pH impedance monitoring. 97 Gastric belches result from transient relaxation of the LES, in contrast to SGB where air sucked or pushed into the esophagus and rapidly expelled, never reaching the stomach. 98 Aerophagia describes air swallowing and typically presents with bloating and increased flatulence rather than belching as the primary symptom. 97 A single center retrospective cohort study determined > 13 SGB over 24 hours on pH impedance monitoring as abnormal, 99 with patients reporting both bothersome belching and other upper GI symptoms, rather than insolated SGB. Reflux events associated with SGB are more likely non-acidic and are often seen in PPI non-responders. 100 , 101 Diaphragmatic breathing, cognitive behavioral therapy, and neuromodulators reduce symptoms and improve quality of life, and antireflux surgery should not be offered for isolated SGB. 102

Rumination syndrome refers to the effortless regurgitation of recently ingested food from the stomach to the oral cavity followed by expectoration or re-mastication and re-swallowing, in the absence of nausea or retching. 103 Rumination episodes, indistinguishable from reflux events, occur in the immediate post prandial period but stop when the regurgitate becomes acidic. While rare in the general population, rumination can be identified in PPI-non responders using post prandial HRM with impedance monitoring, or pH impedance monitoring. 101 , 104 Management consists of patient education, behavioral therapy, and diaphragmatic breathing rather than anti-reflux therapies. 105 , 106

Behavioral disorders can also overlap with GERD, where reflux metrics may be pathologic despite symptom presentations and test findings suggestive of SGB or rumination syndrome. 107 ROLE OF HYPERVIGILANCE

Perception of esophageal stimuli occurs from the complex interplay between visceral afferent nerves in the luminal gut and peripheral nervous system as well as central cognitive and psychological processes. 100 Disturbances in mood or emotional arousal can impair and amplify interpretation of esophageal stimuli. 108 , 109 Hyperawareness of esophageal sensation leads to the perception of stimuli as frightening, and patients can develop a disproportionate behavioral response from catastrophic thinking about potential consequences. The periodic improvement of symptoms may be inappropriately attributed to close selective attention and avoidance of perceived triggers, further reinforcing the behavior pattern. This cognitive-affective pattern is collectively referred to as “esophageal hypervigilance” and can add to PPI refractory symptom burden and significantly impaired quality of life. 13

While understanding of esophageal hypervigilance has evolved over the last decade, the concept of hypervigilance is well established in both mental health and pain disorders. 110 The esophageal hypervigilance and anxiety scale (EHAS) is a 15-item patient reported outcome adapted to the esophagus from validated hypervigilance questionnaires. 111 In the initial validation cohort of 982 patients, EHAS demonstrated excellent internal consistency, reliability, and both total and sub-scores for symptom-specific anxiety and hypervigilance positively correlated with symptom severity and negatively correlated with quality of life. 111 Subsequent studies evaluating patients with reflux symptoms found that EHAS predicts symptom severity regardless of acid burden on ambulatory testing with either pH impedance or prolonged wireless pH monitoring across different reflux phenotypes. 8 , 112 Higher EHAS scores are associated with more severe LPS despite no difference in esophageal reflux metrics. 113 In a study of 102 patients who underwent anti-reflux surgery for GERD, pre-operative EHAS was an independent predictor of both symptom severity before surgery and symptom improvement after surgery. 114

Esophageal hypervigilance offers a novel mechanism to explain discordance between reflux symptoms and physiologic testing and provides additional targets for therapy including cognitive behavioral therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy. 115 , 116 CONCLUSIONS

While GERD evaluation starts with characterization of troublesome symptoms suggested by the Montreal consensus, symptoms alone do not define actionable GERD, although typical symptoms without alarm features may warrant empiric acid suppressive therapy. Mucosal injury phenotypes are identified in a minority of symptomatic patients on upper endoscopy, especially when studied off therapy. When endoscopy is normal or demonstrates LA grade A esophagitis, GERD remains unproven, and ambulatory reflux monitoring can identify or rule out NERD, and potentially diagnose RH, FH and behavioral disorders. Diagnosis of E-DGBI requires exclusion of mucosal injury and abnormal reflux burden phenotypes, identified using Lyon Consensus criteria. Hypervigilance and symptom-specific anxiety, as well as E-DGBI diagnosed using Rome criteria can coexist across all the symptomatic reflux phenotypes. Therefore, Montreal, Lyon and Rome are intricately linked together in patient evaluation, and concepts from each of these contribute to accurate phenotyping and optimal management. 10

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is one of the most frequent gastrointestinal disorders. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are effective in healing lesions and improving symptoms in most cases, although up to 40% of GERD patients do not respond adequately to PPI therapy. Refractory GERD (rGERD) is one of the most challenging problems, given its impact on the quality of life and consumption of health care resources. The definition of rGERD is a controversial topic as it has not been unequivocally established. Indeed, some patients unresponsive to PPIs who experience symptoms potentially related to GERD may not have GERD; in this case the definition could be replaced with “reflux-like PPI-refractory symptoms.” Patients with persistent reflux-like symptoms should undergo a diagnostic workup aimed at finding objective evidence of GERD through endoscopic and pH-impedance investigations. The management strategies regarding rGERD, apart from a careful check of patient's compliance with PPIs, a possible change in the timing of their administration and the choice of a PPI with a different metabolic pathway, include other pharmacologic treatments. These include histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs), alginates, antacids and mucosal protective agents, potassium competitive acid blockers (PCABs), prokinetics, gamma aminobutyric acid-B (GABA-B) receptor agonists and metabotropic glutamate receptor-5 (mGluR5) antagonists, and pain modulators. If there is no benefit from medical therapy, but there is objective evidence of GERD, invasive antireflux options should be evaluated after having carefully explained the risks and benefits to the patient. The most widely performed invasive antireflux option remains laparoscopic antireflux surgery (LARS), even if other, less invasive, interventions have been suggested in the last few decades, including endoscopic transoral incisionless fundoplication (TIF), magnetic sphincter augmentation (LINX) or radiofrequency therapy (Stretta). Due to the different mechanisms underlying rGERD, the most effective strategy can vary, and it should be tailored to each patient. The aim of this paper is to review the different management options available to successfully deal with rGERD.

Keywords: gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), refractory GERD (rGERD), 24-h multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH (MII-pH), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), laparoscopic antireflux surgery (LARS) Introduction

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is one of the most frequent gastrointestinal diseases ( 1 ). It is defined on the basis of both esophageal and extra-esophageal symptoms, and/or lesions resulting from the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. GERD symptoms can be typical, such as heartburn and regurgitation, and atypical, such as chest pain, chronic cough, laryngeal burn, globus, and hoarseness. Therapy is commonly based on proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and alginates as an add-on therapy. PPIs are effective in healing lesions and improving symptoms in most cases ( 2 ). However, there is a significant proportion of patients, ranging from 10 to 40%, whose symptoms do not adequately respond to PPI therapy ( 3 – 6 ). This condition, commonly known as “refractory GERD” (rGERD), represents a major health problem, given its impact on quality of life and consumption of health care resources ( 7 ). The definition of rGERD is controversial as it has never been clearly established ( 8 ). The most commonly used definition is: symptoms (retrosternal heartburn and/or regurgitation) present at least 3 times per week not responding to a double dose of PPIs for 8–12 weeks ( 4 , 7 – 10 ). It must be emphasized that this definition is only clinical, and it does not take into account the need to have objective evidence of GERD based on endoscopic findings and pH-impedance monitoring. Indeed, many patients who experience symptoms potentially related to GERD and not responding to PPI are not really affected by GERD ( 7 , 9 ). In this case the definition could be changed to “reflux-like PPI-refractory symptoms.” The latest ESNM/ANMS consensus paper ( 11 ), in accordance with recent recommendations ( 12 – 14 ), defined “refractory GERD symptoms” as the persistence of symptoms on therapy, in patients with prior objective evidence of GERD (erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, long segment Barrett's esophagus, or abnormal esophageal acid exposure on reflux monitoring performed off therapy) and rGERD as “persistence of GERD symptoms with objective evidence of GERD (through endoscopic and pH-impedance findings) despite optimized PPI therapy over at least 8 weeks.” The complex pathogenetic mechanisms underlying rGERD represent a major challenge in gastroenterological clinical practice and need to be further investigated in order to guide effective therapeutic interventions ( 15 ). The present paper was aimed at reviewing the treatment of rGERD in light of the most recent research.

Clinical tip: rGERD is referred to the persistence of GERD symptoms with objective evidence of GERD despite optimized PPI therapy over at least 8 weeks . Diagnostic Workup Patients with persistent reflux symptoms should undergo a diagnostic pathway aimed at confirming the diagnosis of GERD, evaluating potential comorbidities (including obesity, cardiological and respiratory diseases, psychological/psychiatric disorders) ( 16 ), presence of gut-brain axis disorders ( 17 – 20 ) and the use of concomitant medications ( 21 ) ( Table 1 ). An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), with mucosal biopsies when necessary, should be suggested in order to identify the presence of erosive esophagitis (and its complications) and/or to rule out other causes of esophageal damage, like eosinophilic esophagitis ( 22 , 23 ). If negative, other tests should be performed ( 24 ). High-resolution esophageal manometry (HREM) should be carried out to detect non-reflux esophageal disorders ( 10 , 25 ), such as esophageal motility disorders, which may have similar complaints of patients with GERD ( 26 – 29 ). If symptoms are suspected of being due to delayed gastric emptying, an assessment of gastric emptying (scintigraphy or breath test) is recommended ( 30 , 31 ) ( Table 2 ).

HREM is also mandatory in order to correctly perform a 24-h multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH (MII-pH) monitoring, the current gold standard test to verify the presence of reflux and its association with symptoms ( 13 , 32 , 33 ). MII-pH monitoring assesses the chemical composition of reflux (acidic, weakly acidic, or non-acidic based on pH), its physical composition (liquid, gaseous, or mixed), and its migration to the distal esophagus ( 34 ). This technique, in combination with the analysis of the relationship between symptoms and reflux events [symptom index (SI) or symptom association probability (SAP)], determines the association of reflux events with GERD symptoms ( 7 , 15 , 35 , 36 ). The GERD Consensus Group considers an acid exposure time (AET) to be normal when <4% and pathological when >6%. For borderline values (between 4 and 6%) the Group suggests considering other metrics, e.g., the number of reflux episodes (acidic, weakly acidic or weakly alkaline), where more than 80 reflux episodes per 24 h are definitely considered abnormal. However, it has also been reported that the total number of reflux episodes alone is not sufficient to confirm the diagnosis of GERD and it should be considered only as an exploratory tool ( 13 , 37 ).

MII-pH monitoring leads to a stratification of patients into ongoing acid reflux, ongoing symptomatic non-acid reflux (when AET is normal but the patient reports symptoms corresponding to non-acid or weakly acid reflux events) and non-reflux (when AET is normal and reported symptoms are independent of reflux events) ( 25 , 38 – 41 ). The test carried out “off treatment,” i.e., after having suspended any acid-suppressive therapy for at least 20 days, confirms the diagnosis of GERD (NERD type), discriminating between GERD functional esophageal disorders like reflux hypersensitivity (RH) and functional heartburn (FH) ( 42 ). The latest ESNM/ANMS consensus paper emphasizes the importance of considering additional impedance parameters, such as SAP, post-reflux swallow-induced peristaltic wave index, and mean nocturnal baseline impedance, in order to help identify the patients with rGERD presenting with an inconclusive “off treatment” test ( 11 ). MII-pH performed “on – treatment” (during PPI intake) aims to find the causes of a treatment failure ( 25 , 43 ) and is reserved for patients previously diagnosed with GERD (e.g., affected with Los Angeles Grade C or D esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, or pathological acid exposure off PPI on esophageal pH monitoring) not responsive to an optimized PPI trial. MII-pH monitoring is essential to assess not only a PPI-refractory acid exposure but also an excessive burden of weakly-acidic contents ( 37 ). Identifying the rGERD patient phenotype through MII-pH monitoring is crucial to enable proper management on the basis of the pathophysiological mechanisms ( 25 , 44 ).

Clinical tip: 24 h MII-pH monitoring “on - treatment” is the gold standard in the diagnostic pathway for rGERD, it being crucial in confirming the presence of reflux and its association with symptoms . Potential Causes of rGERD PPI Compliance

In rGERD patients it is necessary to evaluate compliance with the therapy, both in terms of dose and timing of drug intake ( 45 ). Dose and timing are key factors in obtaining an adequate response. PPI should be taken when fasting, at least 30 min before a meal, preferably in the morning before breakfast or, in the case of a second dose in the evening before dinner. This is to achieve maximum gastric acid suppression, blocking the proton pumps before food activates them ( 3 ). Up to 54% of patients take PPI incorrectly ( 46 ) and several studies have shown a poor adherence to PPI therapy, with two reports finding that only 53.8 and 67.7% of patients adhered correctly kept to the prescription for more than 80% of the expected time ( 47 , 48 ). In addition, many patients stop treatment when their symptoms improve. This was shown by a large population survey in which only 55% of patients took PPI once a day for 4 weeks as prescribed, with 37% taking the drug for 12 days or less ( 49 ). Moreover, a study involving 100 patients with persistent GERD-related symptoms found that only 8% of them took the PPI therapy 30–60 min before meals as prescribed ( 47 ). Factors related to poor adherence are mainly the presence of mild symptoms, the onset of side effects, poor information, and poor knowledge on the part of the physician regarding the more detailed pharmacological characteristics of PPIs ( 50 ).
PPI Metabolism

The pharmacological activity of PPIs differs among patients. A potential contributing factor in this regard is the genotypic variability of cytochrome P450 (CYP) ( 51 ). PPIs are metabolized by the liver enzyme complex of CYP, mainly by CYP2C19, and to a lesser extent by CYP3A4. There are three polymorphic variants of CYP2C19 corresponding to 3 different phenotypes: extended or rapid metabolizer (RM) (homozygous, with two mutated alleles), intermediate metabolizer (IM) (heterozygous, one mutated allele and one wildtype) and slow metabolizer (SM) (two wild-type alleles). The rapid metabolizing variant is present in about 60–70% of Caucasians and 30–40% of Asians ( 52 ). In a recent meta-analysis, it was found that the response rate to PPIs in RM is lower (52.2%) than in IM (56.7%) and in SM (61.3%) ( 53 ). The role of CYP2C19 activity is still unclear. There is only one study in which a discrepancy between a single and double dose of Pantoprazole in RMs is observed, and this could represent a starting point for future studies ( 54 ). Up to date genotyping of CYP2C19 is possible by polymeric chain reaction on a peripheral blood sample, but it is not yet widely available for clinical practice ( 55 ).

Different PPI Agents Evidence of the superiority of a PPI agent in comparison with others for rGERD is scarce, but some data suggest that different types of PPI activity can vary widely in terms of acid suppression ( 56 ), so some patients could exhibit significant variability in their clinical response to different molecules. Hence, when considering large cohorts of patients there is no evidence of superiority of one PPI over another, whereas in the individual patient it is sometimes useful to switch to a different PPI to obtain better symptom control ( 57 ). Persistent Weakly Acid or Non-acid Reflux

Stimuli other than strong acidity can also be responsible for reflux symptoms, i.e., weakly acid reflux (WAR) or weakly alkaline reflux (WalkR). WalkR has a pH > 7 and WAR has a pH between 4 and 7. It has been observed that between 30 and 40% of patients with rGERD have symptoms related to events of WAR and WalkR ( 7 – 10 , 15 , 58 – 60 ). It should not be forgotten that in patients taking PPI, reflux episodes are more frequently of weakly acidic and weakly alkaline nature than acidic as a direct consequence of acid suppression ( 35 ). The most widely accepted hypothesis is that distension of the esophagus due to reflux volume and esophageal hypersensitivity to reflux are the conditions that trigger the symptoms ( 61 ). It has also been hypothesized that lower pH values of WAR could be a determinant factor in provoking heartburn ( 39 , 62 , 63 ). During a weakly acidic reflux event, pepsin can migrate into the esophagus. This has a proteolytic effect, and although its maximum activity is between pH 1.9–3.6, it displays partial activity even above pH 6 ( 61 ). Moreover, it has also been observed that up to pH 6.5, mucosal repair may be impaired ( 61 ) and previous exposure of the mucosa to acidic pH may result in the development of hyperalgesia to both mechanical and chemical stimulation ( 64 ).
Duodenogastroesophageal or Bile Reflux

Many physicians confuse WAR and bile reflux. The latter is weakly alkaline and can be found especially in patients who have undergone gastrectomy. Bilirubin and bile acids can damage the esophageal mucosa, causing apoptosis, appearance of dilated intercellular spaces (DIS), and increased mucosal permeability ( 7 , 53 , 65 – 67 ). Data on the role of bile reflux in rGERD are controversial. In a study by de Bortoli et al. bile reflux was shown to play a role in the origin of reflux symptoms not responding to acid suppression ( 68 ). However, Gasiorowka et al. found no difference in the degree of duodenogastroesophageal reflux and acid exposure during treatment between patients who failed to respond and those who achieved complete symptom resolution after a PPI trial ( 69 ).
Pathophysiology of rGERD Antireflux Barrier

The weakening of the physiological antireflux barrier seems to play a role in promoting rGERD ( 3 , 9 ). The antireflux barrier is a high-pressure area consisting of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) attached to the crural diaphragm through the esophageal ligament, and it prevents gastroesophageal reflux. A reduction in the mucosal barrier's integrity is mainly determined by reduced LES resting pressure, especially in the presence of hiatal hernia, and transient relaxation of LES (TLESR), mainly in the presence of an intact hiatus; this may lead to an increase in volume and exposure time of the refluxed material ( 3 , 12 , 21 , 70 ). Zerbib et al. ( 11 ) reiterated the potential contribution of obesity (especially central obesity) in promoting rGERD through increasing gastric pressure, leading to higher TLESR events. Further studies are underway to clarify the importance of a weakening of the antireflux barrier in the pathogenesis of rGERD ( 24 , 71 – 73 ).

Esophageal Clearance It has been observed that a delayed clearance of acid and bolus from the esophagus may be associated with a persistence of pathologic reflux, particularly following conditions such as altered esophageal peristalsis, hiatal hernia, and alterations in salivation ( 74 – 78 ). One study has also observed that PPI- refractory patients have lower basal levels of esophageal clearance, which may worsen the effect of reflux ( 79 ). Delayed Gastric Emptying

The association between delayed gastric emptying and rGERD remains unclear ( 80 ). It has been hypothesized that delayed gastric emptying, or gastroparesis, may contribute to rGERD through increased gastric distension and consequent TLESR events, which promote reflux of gastric content into the esophagus ( 81 ). In one study the use of a prokinetic agent, accelerating gastric emptying prior to pH-impedance, and manometry tests significantly reduced AET and clearance ( 82 ). Esophageal Hypersensitivity and Hypervigilance

There is growing consensus that esophageal hypersensitivity plays an important role in rGERD, particularly in the presence of NAR related symptoms ( 83 , 84 ). It is defined as the increased perception of different kinds of stimuli, including acid, temperature, mechanical distension, and electrical stimulation ( 70 ). The pathophysiologic mechanism seems to involve central and peripheral sensitization through the presence of DIS and exposure of subepithelial nerves to acid. Chronic psychological stress can induce disruption of the intestinal epithelial tight junction proteins, leading to increased intestinal epithelial permeability and associated visceral hyperalgesia ( 7 , 65 – 67 , 84 ). Recently, the new concept of esophageal hypervigilance, defined as the cognitive-affective process that results from over-awareness of the discomfort, was introduced by Keefer et al. ( 85 ) as a possible factor involved in rGERD. The analysis of 70 patients with PPI refractory symptoms studied with pH-impedance and psychometric tests showed that the hypervigilance was shared by all phenotypes, regardless of the patient's phenotype in terms of positive or negative correlation of symptoms and normal or abnormal acid exposure ( 85 ).

Therapy of rGERD As previously described, several different mechanisms can lead to rGERD and therapy should target specific pathophysiological events. However, in clinical practice, drug use is often aimed at controlling refractory symptoms, especially refractory heartburn or refractory epigastric pain ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1. Open in a new tab
